title: The Last Supper
description: Send us Fan Mail   In our journey through the scriptures today, we delve into the profound significance of the Lord's Supper, a divinely ordained memorial that Jesus instituted for His followers. This sacred ordinance, often referred to as Communion, is a simple yet powerful act of remembrance. Unlike grand monuments such as the Lincoln Memorial or the Washington Monument, which stand as towering testaments to historical figures, Jesus chose humble elements—a piece of bread and the juice from a crushed grape—to serve as the enduring symbols of His sacrifice.  The Lord's Supper is a call to remember Jesus, to recover from our spiritual amnesia, and to reflect on the immense cost of our freedom. The bread symbolizes His body given for us, and the juice represents His blood shed to establish a new covenant. This act of remembrance is not just a ritual; it is a profound spiritual exercise that reconnects us with the core of our faith. Every time we partake in this ordinance, we are reminded of the One who gave everything for our redemption.  Memorials have always played a significant role in human history, serving as reminders of important events and individuals. Memorial Day, for instance, was established to honor soldiers who died in the American Civil War and later expanded to include all military personnel who have served the country. Similarly, ancient cultures, like the Vikings, had their own memorial ceremonies to honor fallen warriors. These acts of remembrance are deeply ingrained in our collective consciousness.  The Lincoln Memorial, with its 29-foot-tall statue of Abraham Lincoln and inscriptions of his Gettysburg Address and inaugural addresses, serves as a powerful reminder of his legacy. The Washington Monument, with its 897 steps and various memorial stones, including one inscribed with "Laus Deo" (Praise be to God), stands as a testament to the nation's first president. These monuments are designed to be permanent, etched in stone, so that future generations can remember the sacrifices and contributions of these great leaders.  However, the most enduring memorial of all is the one instituted by Jesus during the Last Supper. As we read in Luke 22:14-23, Jesus gathered His disciples for a final meal before His crucifixion. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me." He then took a cup of wine and said, "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood." These simple elements—bread and wine—carry profound spiritual significance.  Jesus' choice of these elements is deeply symbolic. The bread, representing His body, signifies the affliction and suffering He endured for our sake. The wine, symbolizing His blood, points to the new covenant that offers eternal atonement for sin. This new covenant, unlike the old one established through the blood of sacrificial animals, is based entirely on Jesus' sacrifice. It is a covenant of grace, dependent solely on Christ's finished work on the cross.  The Lord's Supper is not a re-sacrificing of Jesus, as some traditions might suggest. It is an ordinance of remembrance, a way for believers to continually recall the sacrifice that secured their redemption. By partaking in this meal, we are reminded of our union with Christ and our communion with one another. It is a time to give thanks, to reflect on the cost of our freedom, and to renew our commitment to follow Jesus.  The Lord's Supper is a divinely ordained memorial that transcends time and space. It is a simple yet profound act that calls us to remember Jesus, to reflect on His sacrifice, and to give thanks for the redemption He secured for us. As we partake in this sacred ordinance, let us do so with hearts full of gratitude, minds focused on His sacrifice, and spirits renewed in our commitment to follow Him. title: Bringing God to Life Part 2 (Titus 3:8)
description: Share a comment   “Engage in good deeds” sounds simple until you realize Paul repeats it like a drumbeat and then adds a surprising command: be careful about it. We dig into what that means and why it matters for everyday Christian living, not as performative niceness, but as the gospel made visible through action. The aim isn’t to trade doctrine for activism, it’s to let good doctrine become a life of application that benefits real people in practical ways.   We talk about the mindset shift from random acts of kindness to intentional, thoughtful service, and we break down a three-part formula that sticks: intentionality plus creativity plus initiative. That kind of person shows up early, stays late, takes the distasteful chore, and quietly makes life better for everyone around them. We also get uncomfortably practical about the local church: if any place should be overflowing with volunteers, generosity, and “ready for every good deed” energy, it’s the household of faith.   Then we widen the lens to culture and history. Christians have a track record of doing good works that are genuinely “profitable” for all people, including unbelievers, from caring for abandoned children to building early health care systems to staying with the sick during plagues. We close with stories that capture the goal: living faith so tangibly that someone looks you in the eye and asks, “Where can I get a heart like yours?” If this challenges you, share it with a friend, subscribe for more, and leave a review, then tell us what one good deed you’re going to start this week. title: Bringing God to Life Part 1 (Titus 3:8)
description: Share a comment   A gorgeous church building. Onion-shaped turrets. A familiar lobby. Then the doors open and the sanctuary is stacked floor to ceiling with chicken coops. The official tour guide smiles and says, “God is not real. Chickens are real.” That one line captures the tension so many of us feel today: the pressures of life are concrete, immediate, and loud, while faith can get pushed into the background like it’s just an idea.  We work through Titus 3:8 where Paul tells Titus to speak confidently, like a coach calling the play with no time left on the clock. We trace why the gospel is a “trustworthy statement” and revisit the core of grace: God’s kindness in Christ, salvation by faith rather than deeds, the cleansing and renewal of the Holy Spirit, and justification that cancels the charges against us. We also talk honestly about the temptation for pastors, teachers, and everyday Christians to avoid hard lines because culture feels hostile or because we want to please people.  Then Paul’s focus sharpens: this is for “those who have believed God” and that belief is personal. God isn’t watching from a distance. He is near, knowable, and involved. And that personal reality leads to a public lifestyle that is “truly beneficial” to others. We dig into why Christians don’t do good deeds to earn heaven, but because grace changes what we want, and because visible kindness gets the world’s attention in a way religious talk often doesn’t. title: Ambushed by Goodness Part 2 (Titus 3:4–7)
description: Share a comment   Being “born again” can sound like religious slang until you slow down and ask what the Bible actually means by it. We take Titus 3 and trace three loaded words that reshape everything: regeneration, renewal, and justification. The claim is simple and disruptive: the Holy Spirit gives a full internal cleansing, Jesus Christ pays in full, and grace leaves us with nothing to boast about and everything to be grateful for.  We also tackle a common point of confusion with real pastoral clarity: where does baptism fit? We talk about why the early church treats baptism as the normal next step of obedience, and why that still does not make baptism the mechanism of salvation. When you make any ritual a requirement for being saved, you quietly add a human contribution to a rescue that Scripture describes as God’s work from start to finish.  Then we go deeper into what changes after the new birth. Regeneration is a moment, but renewal is a lifetime, including the daily battle to resist being pressed into the world’s mold and instead letting God reshape our minds through His Word. We close with a vivid picture of justification that feels like a courtroom scene: God doesn’t simply cut us a break, He credits us with Christ’s spotless record and promises us the hope of eternal life as heirs. title: Ambushed by Goodness Part 1 (Titus 3:4–7)
description: Share a comment   One surprise announcement can change everything: a stranger pays a debt you could never erase. We use that real story of six-figure student loans forgiven on the spot to open up a bigger reality the Bible calls grace. When Paul writes Titus 3:4-7, he describes people like us at our worst, then turns the entire sentence on one small word: “but.” What comes next is the heart of the gospel, the kindness of God appearing to save.  We talk about what “kindness” and “love for mankind” actually mean, including the idea of divine philanthropy. Not the celebrity kind that writes a check, but the ultimate gift of self-giving love through the incarnation, Jesus coming near rather than pitying us from far away. Along the way we challenge the stubborn myth that salvation is God helping our best effort. Titus is blunt: he saves “not on the basis of deeds,” but “according to his mercy,” leaving no room for spiritual bragging and every reason for gratitude.  Then we dig into what happens after rescue: “the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.” We clarify why baptism is a powerful public sign but not the mechanism of salvation, and why the Spirit’s work is a deep internal cleansing, not a quick spot clean. title: Remember! Part 2 (Titus 3:3–4)
description: Share a comment   “I want that shade… and that shade… and that shade.” We start with a line that sounds funny until it exposes something deadly serious: covetousness does not just tempt us, it trains us. The more we chase, the less we’re satisfied, and what feels like freedom turns into a quiet kind of bondage. We walk through why materialism and hedonism are not side issues but symptoms of a deeper problem of the heart, where desire becomes a master and contentment starts to feel impossible.  From there, we zoom out to the culture around us. When a society loses a moral compass, it reaches for rules and bans while still struggling to answer the basic question: who gets to define right and wrong? Stories about academic cheating, shifting boundaries, and moral confusion point to a sobering reality: when we dismiss God’s authority, we don’t drift into neutrality. We drift into belligerence, and we end up tangled in contradictions we can’t solve with policy alone.  Then we take the turn Titus 3 is famous for. Right after the list of what we were, we get one of the most hopeful words in Scripture: “But.” The kindness of God appears, not to discard us, but to save us. We close with the unforgettable Eddie Rickenbacker story, a living picture of what it looks like to spend your life saying “thank you.”  If this sparked conviction or hope, subscribe, share this with a friend, and leave a review. title: Remember! Part 1 (Titus 3:3–4)
description: Share a comment   Kindness feels scarce right now, and it is tempting to answer sarcasm with sarcasm and insults with “just telling the truth.” We go to Titus 3 because Paul refuses to let believers drift into the mood of the age. That is not weakness. It is gospel strength on display.  Stephen Davey then shows where that kind of kindness actually comes from, and the answer is humbling. Paul points us back to our own story: “we also once were” foolish, disobedient, deceived, and enslaved. We talk through what that means in plain terms, including foolishness as intentional bias against God, disobedience as belligerence toward any moral authority, deception as spiritual blindness, and bondage to “various lusts and pleasures” that can include fantasies, hedonism, and even materialism. If you are tired of angry Christianity or tired of your own reactions, this message offers a better path: remember the pit you were rescued from, and let gratitude reshape your tone, your habits, and your relationships. title: Living in the City of Man Part 2 (Titus 3:1–2)
description: Share a comment   Rome didn’t need another angry letter. It needed a different kind of person. We pick up in Titus 3 and ask what it looks like to represent the city of God while living in the city of man, especially when the surrounding culture feels morally upside down and authority feels frustrating. Stephen walks through why early Christians became known as “remarkable” people, not because they had power, but because their character refused to look like the status quo.  We talk candidly about submission to government and where the line is drawn: we obey the law until the law demands we violate the Word of God. From there, the message turns painfully practical. What is my attitude toward parents, teachers, supervisors, pastors, local leaders, taxes, and even that red light when nobody else is on the road? The goal isn’t a polished image. It’s a heart that trusts God enough to live with integrity. title: Living in the City of Man Part 1 (Titus 3:1–2)
description: Share a comment   The pressure to quit on culture is real and it is growing. When you watch faith mocked, morality redefined, and even public prayer treated like a problem, it can feel easier to pull back into a safe Christian bubble. We push against that impulse with a surprising biblical reminder: God didn’t save us and immediately take us to heaven because He wants our lives, right here, to demonstrate the reality of the City of God while we live in the City of Man.  Stephen Davy opens a new series in the book of Titus called “Remarkable Christianity” and starts with Titus 3:1, where Paul commands believers to be subject to rulers and authorities. That is not a suggestion, and it is not reserved for “good governments.” We talk about why Christians are not above the law, what civic duty looks like in everyday life, and how fear and resentment can signal that we have forgotten God’s providence. Instead of panic, we learn to engage, speak with clarity, and serve our communities as salt and light.  Then we go deeper into the hardest question: what happens when authority is hostile to the gospel? Paul wrote under Nero, in a morally chaotic society, yet the early church grew because Christians lived distinctly and respectfully. We also draw the line Scripture draws: when a law demands that we violate God’s Word, we obey God rather than man. title: Settling for Sand (Luke 6:46-49)
description: Share a comment   Two houses can look identical until the river rises. title: Christianity Behind the Curtain (Luke 6:38-45)
description: Share a comment   If you have ever looked around and thought, “I can’t believe they did that,” Jesus has a way of turning the mirror back toward us. First, genuine generosity that goes beyond money and shows up in time, service, hospitality, and an open-handed attitude toward people in need. Then we hear a caution about conformity: the spiritually blind cannot lead the spiritually blind, and disciples eventually become like their teachers. title: Every Reason to Judge (Luke 6:37)
description: Share a comment   “Judge not” might be the most quoted Bible line in public arguments and one of the least understood. From there, we ask the hard question people avoid: is it ever right to judge? We trace the Bible’s own boundaries and show why Christians must be able to call sin what it is, evaluate teaching for truth or error, and practice honest self-examination. We talk about church accountability, the difference between repentant struggle and unrepentant defiance, and why “tolerance” can sometimes be a mask for arrogance. We also address the modern instinct to judge by vibes, appearances, and assumed motives, and why Scripture insists that only God can fully expose what’s hidden in the heart.  We close with a practical path toward what we call gracious discernment: staying hungry for wisdom, committing to obeying what we learn, saturating our minds with God’s Word, and putting truth into practice until maturity becomes instinct. We talk about what this looks like when the pressure is real, including stories of persecuted believers and the reminder that the church has always had to live faithfully in hostile environments. From generosity to the Golden Rule to loving enemies, the thread is consistent: Jesus isn’t calling us to imitate humanity, but to imitate God, who is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. We end with clear encouragement to rise above arguments, consider stepping away from social media, and re-center on the Great Commission over political wins, because making disciples has eternal weight. title: Warning Signs (Luke 6:24-26)
description: Share a comment   The most dangerous warning signs aren’t always in the sky or the headlines. Sometimes they show up as comfort, confidence, and applause. The rainbow stands as a sign of mercy, but the lesser-quoted promise is just as grounding: while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not cease. In a culture fueled by fear and control, that promise calls us to trust God’s rule over creation while still taking sin, truth, and accountability seriously. title: Remember to Remember! (2 Peter 1:12-15)
description: Share a comment   Drift is terrifying precisely because it feels harmless at first. One small compromise, one missed habit, one quiet season of neglect, and before you know it you are farther from spiritual clarity than you ever planned to be. We talk candidly about spiritual drift and mission drift, starting with the everyday places people slide: morality, trust in Scripture, private prayer, responsibilities at home and work, and the slow loss of personal pursuit of God.   Then we zoom out to institutional drift with a sobering look at Christian roots in American higher education. When founding documents celebrate Christ, but later generations remove those commitments from diplomas and curriculum, you get a real-world picture of how a mission can be diluted over time. That warning is not meant to shame the past. It is meant to wake us up to how easily any godly endeavor can be pulled off course if we stop guarding the purpose.   Finally, we land in 2 Peter 1 where Peter presses one word again and again: remember. We break down three practical reminders for Christian discipleship and spiritual growth: truth must be applied, not merely learned; the brevity of life should motivate urgent faithfulness; and true success is measured by godly influence, not affluence. title: The Finishing Touch Part 2 (2 Peter 1:7b)
description: Share a comment   Anger that flares up and “passes in seconds” can still scorch a relationship for days. We dig into Paul’s blunt line from 1 Corinthians 13, “love is not irritable,” and the original word picture behind it: an eruption, a paroxysm, an explosion of fury. The point is not behavior polish or white-knuckle self-control. Real Christian love is Spirit-formed, and it changes what comes out of us when we are pressured, disappointed, or flat-out annoyed.  We also reframe a passage many people only hear at weddings. 1 Corinthians 13 is written to Christians of every age and season, and it delivers a surprising test of spiritual maturity: you can speak brilliantly, know Scripture deeply, and even tell the truth accurately, yet still accomplish nothing lasting if you don’t love the people in front of you. Paul’s “clanging cymbal” image becomes painfully relevant for how we talk, correct, post, and respond, especially in a culture trained toward self-promotion, envy, and keeping score.  Then we walk through what agape does and does not do, with practical, searchable takeaways for Christian relationships, marriage help, church unity, and personal discipleship: patient and kind together, not envious, not boastful, not puffed up, not rude, not insisting on its own way. We spend meaningful time on resentment as “counting up wrongdoing,” trading the ledger for a well-worn eraser, and learning to rejoice with the truth rather than celebrate sin. The closing turn lands on the gospel itself: God’s agape love in giving his Son, and how our love starts to resemble his when we surrender control to the Spirit. title: The Finishing Touch Part 1 (2 Peter 1:7b)
description: Share a comment   If “love” is everywhere, why does it feel so thin? We dig into agape, the kind of love Scripture treats as the finishing touch of spiritual maturity and the one quality that keeps everything else from going off the rails. Peter’s list in 2 Peter 1 stacks up virtues like knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, and godliness, then lands on love as the crown. We talk about why that matters: without agape, knowledge quietly turns into pride, virtue hardens into legalism, and perseverance becomes self-preservation.  We also slow down and compare the common Greek words for love. Storge is family affection, philia is friendship built on shared interests, and eros is sexual desire that needs commitment to avoid becoming selfish and disposable. Then we get to the surprise: the New Testament keeps choosing agape, a word the surrounding culture barely used, because it points to a supernatural, learned way of living that doesn’t rise naturally in us.  From there we step into 1 Corinthians 13 and let Paul confront us. You can be gifted, eloquent, and loaded with Bible knowledge, but without love you’re just making noise, and without love you’re nothing. That lens changes how we speak, how we serve, and even how we post online, where bragging can become “helpful content” and envy can hide behind a smile. title: Keep Swimming! (2 Peter 1:6)
description: Share a comment   Pressure has a way of stripping life down to what’s real. description: Share a comment   “Just say no” sounded simple, looked impressive, and still didn’t change hearts. We dig into why those famous behavior campaigns failed and how that same mistake shows up when we treat self-control like a slogan instead of a deeper kind of formation. If you’ve ever thought, “Why do I keep snapping, scrolling, or spiraling when I know better?” this conversation is for you.  We work through 2 Peter 1 and the call to “supplement” saving faith with virtue, practical knowledge, and self-control. We talk about what self-control actually means in the Bible: dominion over yourself, staying composed, holding yourself in. Then we take it out of the classroom and into real life, where impatience flares in grocery lines, traffic, and tense conversations. Along the way, we look at Acts 24 and Paul’s direct challenge to Felix and Drusilla, a reminder that the gospel doesn’t dodge the obvious pressure points in our lives.  We also face the modern pressure cooker. Technology trains us to expect everything instantly, shrinking patience to a few seconds and teaching both kids and adults to avoid discomfort instead of mastering it. The good news is that Christian self-control is not just saying no. It’s also saying yes: a daily surrender to the Holy Spirit, keeping in step with him, and learning to present ourselves to God instead of our impulses. title: The Right Kind of Gold Rush (2 Peter 1:5a)
description: Share a comment   Every day, people make choices that look “normal” on the surface but add up to a life that quietly falls apart. We start with sobering youth statistics and the raw question behind them: if you believe you’re an accident in an accidental universe, what real reason is there to say no to the easy escape, the quick thrill, or the crowd’s approval?  From there, we pivot to the California Gold Rush and the surprising detail most folks miss: the biggest fortunes often went to the people who equipped the miners, not the miners themselves. That history becomes a vivid picture of our own 21st century gold rush for stuff, status, and self, and it sets up the central challenge of the conversation: wisdom is calling just as loudly, and it offers a treasure better than gold.  We dig into 2 Peter 1:5 and Proverbs 1:7 to define biblical knowledge as practical, decision-shaping understanding rooted in the fear of the Lord. Not trivia. Not raw intelligence. A kind of Christian maturity that becomes visible in everyday choices, humility, and teachability. We also contrast that path with Proverbs’ portrait of the “fool,” showing how arrogance, shallowness, resistance to correction, and living unaccountable to God can wreck a life even when someone looks successful on paper. The episode closes with a story that will make you rethink how you treat your Bible and why you cannot live out what you have not learned. title: The Passionate Pursuit of Excellence (2 Peter 1:5a)
description: Share a comment   Politicians love to talk about “values,” especially in an election year, but that word can hide a problem: what we value is not always virtuous, and what feels “right” can quietly be deadly. We start with a simple reframe that cuts through the noise. The biggest question isn’t how long you’re going to live. It’s how you’re going to live, and whether your life is actually meaningful.  We open 2 Peter 1 and treat Peter’s list like a divinely designed supplement program for spiritual growth: faith supplemented with virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. Then we slow down and sit with the promise attached to it. When these qualities are yours and increasing, they keep you from becoming ineffective and unfruitful in the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Peter even adds a warning-turned-invitation: practice these qualities and you “will never fall,” not as a threat of losing salvation, but as a rescue from a wasted, miserable, self-centered Christian life.  From there we get practical about sanctification and daily discipleship. God has already provided the resources, but we still have to steer the car and build on the foundation. We also dig into the first supplement, virtue, not as vague niceness but as excellence, doing what God assigned you with real care, whether anyone notices or not. The final challenge gets personal: if you had one month to live, what would you start doing, stop doing, and pursue with urgency? title: Rafting On Whitewater (2 Peter 1:3-4)
description: Share a comment   White water will tell you what you really trust. We open with a rafting story that feels uncomfortably familiar: the raft flips, panic hits, and the “safe” move looks like swimming to the calm edge. Then comes the twist. The quiet water is where the danger hides, and the rough water is where protection and forward motion actually live. That picture becomes a direct challenge to how we respond to pressure, suffering, and temptation in everyday Christian life.   From 2 Peter 1:3-4, we lay out two solid assurances for believers who feel displaced, squeezed, or tired: God’s divine power has granted us everything we need for life and godliness, and God has also granted us precious and very great promises. We slow down on what “granted” means, why these are permanent resources, and how spiritual growth comes through knowing Jesus Christ as he reveals himself in Scripture, not a made-up version of faith. Finally, we trace the two outcomes Peter describes: growing into Christlike character and escaping the world’s corruption, one decisive “no” at a time. title: The Crowded Life (2 Peter 1:2)
description: Share a comment   Noise is not just annoying, it is formative. When the headlines never stop and the notifications keep buzzing, our minds and hearts get pulled into a current of the sensational, the trivial, and the temporary. We want peace, but we often chase it by trying to quiet the world, and the world will not cooperate. So we go to Peter’s opening prayer in 2 Peter 1:2 and ask a better question: what if the answer is not less trouble, but more grace and peace, multiplied?  We unpack what Peter means by “multiplied” and why he writes this to believers who already have grace and peace in Christ. Then we get specific about grace: God’s favor toward the undeserving, the difference between common grace and saving grace, and the warning about “cheap grace” that keeps a person comfortable but unchanged. From there, we trace what multiplying grace looks like on the ground: handling hardship with glad contentment and answering critics with kindness, with speech seasoned by grace instead of fueled by outrage.  Peace is just as practical. It is not the absence of pressure, but the abiding presence of Christ, a steady heart that comes from an upward focus. That leads to the key that ties everything together: knowledge. Not trivia, not religious facts, but deepening, personal knowledge of God and Jesus through Scripture, the one book that reveals him. We close by getting honest about distractions and building guardrails so the noise does not crowd out the Word.  If you want spiritual growth, biblical encouragement, and real practices for Christian living in a distracted world, listen through to the end. title: What to Remember With 30 Seconds to Live (2 Peter 1:1b)
description: Share a comment   Saying “Jesus is Savior” can sound harmless until you say it like the apostles meant it: Jesus Christ alone. That single word exposes why culture can tolerate vague spirituality but lashes out at biblical Christianity. We talk candidly about what happens when a believer takes a public moral stand, from angry emails and workplace complaints to legal pressure and, at the extreme, violence. The point is not fear or outrage. The point is readiness.  We reflect on how Christians respond when the temperature rises: we learn the truth, we speak with boldness, we stay gracious and patient, we remain reasonable when the world is unreasonable, and we love enemies enough to pray for them and share the gospel persuasively. We also widen the frame to global Christian persecution and the long history of suffering in the church, from Stephen in Acts to believers who are reviled and harmed today.  Then we move into 2 Peter 1:1 for the kind of backbone persecuted Christians need. We unpack saving faith versus everyday faith, why saving faith is a gift we obtain rather than earn, and why it is the object, not the amount, that saves. title: The Final Song Part 2 (1 Chronicles 28-29)
description: Share a comment   The hardest spiritual test is not hearing God say “no” to a bad idea, it’s hearing Him say “no” to a good one. We sit with King David at the end of his life as he looks straight at an unfulfilled dream: he spent years planning a temple for God’s glory, only to watch the assignment pass to Solomon. Instead of bitterness, David gives us a rare picture of maturity: honest desire, real disappointment, and a steady “yet” that keeps trusting God’s wisdom.  From there, we move into a surprisingly practical blueprint for Christian parenting and spiritual leadership. David, a man with public wins and private failures, speaks to his son with clarity: know the God of your father, serve Him with a whole heart, seek Him, be strong, and do the work. We talk about why that personal faith matters more than a “successful life” checklist, and how a parent’s real repentance can carry more weight than perfect performance.  We also unpack David’s public prayer in 1 Chronicles 28 to 29, where stewardship and worship meet. He reminds us that generosity starts with humility because everything we bring to God already came from His hand. And he prays for Solomon’s integrity, not comfort, pushing back on the fantasy that God’s best plan is always the easiest path.  If you’ve ever felt the sting of a delayed dream, a redirected calling, or a parenting moment you wish you could redo, this conversation will help you reset your priorities and reclaim a worshipful perspective. title: Do Babies Really Go To Heaven Part 2 (2 Samuel 12:14-23)
description: Share a comment   The question isn’t academic if you’ve ever held an ultrasound photo, walked out of a hospital empty-handed, or wondered what God does with the smallest lives. We take the most tender and controversial question head-on: do miscarried, stillborn, aborted, and newborn children go to heaven, and what does the Bible actually say?  We start with Romans 5, tracing the contrast between Adam’s disobedience and Jesus Christ’s obedience, and why Paul’s “many will be made righteous” can’t be reduced to a narrow, adult-only category. From there we tackle the foundational claims underneath the whole debate: life begins at God-ordained conception, every human being lives forever because we’re made in the image of God, and the real issue becomes where we live forever.  Then we test popular answers against Scripture. We push back on post-mortem salvation using Luke 16, and we examine baptismal regeneration claims (including household baptism arguments) to ask whether any ceremony can guarantee heaven. Finally, we walk through the grace-versus-works tension: saved by grace alone, yet condemned with reference to willful rebellion and suppressed truth (Romans 1). That framework shapes how we think about “age of accountability” as a state of moral awareness, not a magic number.  If you’re grieving, questioning, or trying to think clearly as a Christian, this conversation is for you. title: Do Babies Really Go To Heaven Part 1 (2 Samuel 12:14-23)
description: Share a comment   One sentence can stop a grieving parent cold: “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.” We start there, with David and Bathsheba in 2 Samuel 12, because the death of a child forces honest Christians to face the hardest pastoral question people ask through tears: did my baby go to heaven?  We don’t reach for a Hallmark answer, and we don’t pretend the Bible offers a single easy proof text for the miscarried, the aborted, the stillborn, or the severely mentally disabled. Instead, we do what careful biblical theology requires: compare passages, connect doctrines, and follow the clues. Psalm 139 takes us into the womb where God “knits” a unique life together, and Jeremiah’s language shows God speaking to an unborn person with purpose and destiny. title: Telling The Truth To God (Psalm 51)
description: Share a comment   Shame makes smart people act like fugitives. Sometimes the hiding is obvious, like a new name and a new city. Sometimes it’s quieter, like a carefully managed story, a tight smile, and a private fear that the truth will catch up. We start with the real account of Katherine Power, who lived for decades under an assumed identity after a bank robbery went wrong and a police officer was killed. When she finally turned herself in, she explained why: she was tired of living with shame, hiddenness, and guilt. That one sentence opens a bigger conversation about what it really takes to come clean.  From there, we walk straight into Psalm 51 and listen to David do the hardest thing a sinner can do: stop defending and start confessing. We organize the psalm around five simple words that map the journey back to God: petition, admission, origin, restoration, and resolution. You’ll hear why David appeals to mercy and steadfast love instead of “a fair shake,” why blot out, wash, and cleanse describe different depths of forgiveness, and why real confession refuses excuses that subtly blame family, circumstances, or even God.  We also talk about the roots beneath the actions. David goes beyond “I sinned” to “I am a sinner,” naming the deeper problem of a corrupted nature. That honesty sets up real hope: restoration is not self-improvement, it’s a miracle of renewal, a clean conscience, and a new heart. We close with David’s resolve to turn forgiveness outward, teaching others the way back and turning grace into a song the whole community can sing.  If you want language for true repentance, a clearer picture of mercy, and a practical way to stop hiding, press play. title: The Cover Up Part 2 (2 Samuel 11:6-27)
description: Share a comment   One bad choice rarely stays lonely. We walk through the David and Bathsheba narrative in 2 Samuel 11 at the exact moment David tries to outsmart consequences, and we watch his options shrink until he starts sacrificing other people to protect his image. We break the spiral into the episode’s four moves: stay calm, apply pressure, conspire to kill, keep up appearances. Uriah becomes the unexpected mirror in the story, a man so committed to duty and brotherhood that he will not go home even when the king tempts him and even when wine is used to lower his guard. title: Governed By Lessor Passions Part 2 (2 Samuel 11:1-5 )
description: Share a comment   Temptation doesn’t walk into your life carrying a warning label. It shows you the highlight reel, then asks you to decide fast. We start with that brutal reality and follow it straight into one of the most sobering moments in Scripture: King David, at the peak of success, choosing comfort over duty, boredom over vigilance, and desire over wisdom, until one look becomes a chain of choices he can’t control.  We slow down in 2 Samuel 11 and connect the dots: why idleness makes us vulnerable, how lust escalates, and why David’s private compromises set the stage for public collapse. The details matter, including the warnings he receives, the cold, transactional way the encounter is recorded, and the two-word message that forces consequences into the open. title: At The Table Of Grace Part 2 (2 Samuel 9 )
description: Share a comment   A new king usually cleans house. David does the opposite. We walk through the tension of the search, the slippery role of Ziba, and the haunting detail that the last heir is “crippled in his feet.” Instead of treating weakness as a deal-breaker, David’s only question is the one grace always asks: where is he? title: When The Answer Is No Part 2 (2 Samuel 7)
description: Share a comment   God says “no” to David, and it’s not because David’s motives are wrong. That’s what makes the moment so unsettling. We follow the story all the way through the emotional turn of one small word: “but.” The plans change, the path shifts, and the question becomes painfully practical: how do we respond when God closes the door? We lay out five responses modeled by David that reshape Christian living and spiritual growth in real time: humility instead of protest, gratitude that trusts God’s longer timeline, surrender that rests in being God’s servant, praise that chooses worship over wrestling, and readiness that stays alert for the window God opens next. Along the way, we talk about contentment as something learned, not wished for, and why trying to “force the locks” only drains faith.   Then we land on the surprising beauty of preparation. David can’t hammer one nail into the temple, but he spends years organizing, gathering resources, and setting Solomon up to succeed without becoming bitter. It’s a picture of faithful obedience, Christian leadership, and trusting the will of God even when the work will outlive you. title: The Last Meal Part 2 (1 Samuel 28 & 31)
description: Share a comment   God’s silence can feel mysterious until you realize what King Saul refuses to face: you can’t demand closeness with God while you’re actively protecting the sin you already know needs confession. We walk through Saul’s final descent and why his complaint “God won’t answer me” isn’t a puzzle, it’s a mirror. Along the way, we use a painfully funny illustration about a man hiding a lit cigarette from his pastor to expose how often we try to “stuff” disobedience out of sight while still asking for guidance, comfort, and clarity.  From there, the story turns darker and stranger as Saul seeks out the medium at Endor. We unpack the reality of the unseen spiritual world without sensationalizing it, and we talk candidly about spiritual deception: why evil doesn’t know the future the way God does, how it can still manipulate with real information, and why chasing supernatural shortcuts can pull us away from God’s revealed Word. We also explain why the passage reads most naturally as a genuine appearance of Samuel delivering God’s final message to Saul.  Then comes the gut punch: a 48-hour death notice. Saul is handed a last mercy window, yet he chooses denial and control, marching toward the outcome he’s been warned about. That leads us to the bigger contrast that closes the message with hope: Saul’s death looks like the end of Israel’s future, but it opens the way for David’s line and ultimately the Messiah. Jesus Christ’s death looks like the end of spiritual hope, but it becomes the doorway to the church, saving grace, and a coming kingdom for unlikely people like us. title: Storm Clouds Part 2 (1 Samuel 19-20)
description: Share a comment   Have you ever felt like life turned against you for no good reason? You did the right thing, obeyed God, and served faithfully, only to watch storm clouds gather where the sun had just been shining. What do you do when doing right leads to being hunted?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 19 and 20 and continues his series on the life of David. The pretense is finally over. King Saul openly orders his son and servants to kill David. Stephen walks you through the crushing losses David absorbs in rapid succession. His position, his wife, his spiritual mentor, and finally his closest friend, Jonathan. Stephen also draws in the courageous witness of Jonathan, a son who refused to imitate his father's evil, and points to David's honest cries in Psalm 59 as the very songs forged in these dark days. Alongside David's story, Stephen brings you into 2 Corinthians 4, where Paul confesses he too has been pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and knocked down, yet never crushed, driven to despair, forsaken, or destroyed. God, who raised us up, wants us to stand. And He wants us to remember how.  This message will comfort your heart when the storm refuses to lift. Desperate times have a way of redefining your sources of strength and rewriting your list of priorities. Every roof will leak except the roof of your Sovereign shelter. Look up. Look ahead. What you see now is not all there is. God will make everything right, even if He waits until glory. Until then, keep singing the song of faith that is being forged in your own hideout. Stephen walks you through the crushing losses David absorbs in rapid succession. His position, his wife, his spiritual mentor, and finally his closest friend, Jonathan. Every layer of stability is stripped away, not because David sinned, but because he stood faithfully in the will of God.  Stephen also draws in the courageous witness of Jonathan, a son who refused to imitate his father's evil, and points to David's honest cries in Psalm 59 as the very songs forged in these dark days. Alongside David's story, Stephen brings you into 2 Corinthians 4, where Paul confesses he too has been pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and knocked down, yet never crushed, driven to despair, forsaken, or destroyed. God, who raised us up, wants us to stand. And He wants us to remember how.  This message will comfort your heart when the storm refuses to lift. Desperate times have a way of redefining your sources of strength and rewriting your list of priorities. Every roof will leak except the roof of your Sovereign shelter. Look up. Look ahead. What you see now is not all there is. God will make everything right, even if He waits until glory. Until then, keep singing the song of faith that is being forged in your own hideout. title: Behaving Wisely Part 2 (1 Samuel 18:1-30)
description: Share a comment   Have you ever wondered what wisdom really looks like in the middle of ordinary life? Not the wisdom of clever answers or shrewd strategies, but the kind that shapes how you respond to praise, criticism, promotion, and setbacks. What does godly wisdom actually look like in flesh and blood?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 18 and continues his series on the life of David. Fresh from defeating Goliath, David is suddenly a national hero. Songs are sung in his honor. Jonathan gives him his own robe and sword. Everyone loves him. But behind the celebration, King Saul begins to boil with envy. Stephen walks you through this chapter and shows how David quietly displays three defining marks of wisdom while Saul digresses into hostility and hatred.  First, walking wisely means responding to promotion with humility. David rises to command, yet he never boasts, never gloats, and never rubs his success in anyone's face. Second, walking wisely means tolerating the weaknesses of others with grace. When Saul hurls spears at him, David does not pick them up and throw them back. He offers the benefit of the doubt and refuses to join the downward spiral of hurt, hate, hostility, and harm. Third, walking wisely means surrendering to the providence of God without complaint. David is demoted, denied a promised bride, and then handed a deadly dowry, yet he keeps trusting the Lord and refuses to defend his own honor.  This message will reshape how you handle both the applause and the arrows in your own life. You do not have to answer every insult. You do not have to defend every slight. You do not have to grasp for what God has not yet given. Walk humbly. Extend grace. Trust the God who is quietly writing your story. title: David and the Sitting Duck Part 2 (1 Samuel 17)
description: Share a comment   Have you always heard the story of David and Goliath as a message about overcoming your personal giants? What if that popular reading actually misses the whole point of what happened in the Valley of Blood?  In this episode, Stephen Davey opens 1 Samuel 17 and walks you through one of the most familiar accounts in Scripture with fresh clarity. Israel is not just facing a military crisis. They are facing a spiritual one. The armies are paralyzed by fear because they have forgotten their God. Even King Saul, once head and shoulders above every other man in Israel, cannot answer the taunts of a nine foot nine inch Philistine warrior. Stephen carefully sets the scene, describing Goliath's armor and weapons in vivid detail, then shows how the entire conflict pivots on how the battle is being seen.  The soldiers see a giant. David sees a blasphemer. The soldiers see an insult against Israel. David sees an insult against the living God. Stephen walks you through four scenes in the chapter. The front lines, the fear, the folly of trying to fight Goliath like Goliath, and the faith of a young shepherd who trusted the Lord's power over his own strength. David refused to wear Saul's armor. He refused to fight on the world's terms. He picked up his sling and stones and stepped into the valley with one all consuming passion. The glory of the God of Israel.  This message will realign your perspective on the battles you face. Don't let your faith depend on majority opinion. Don't let your talents be depreciated by conventional wisdom. And don't let your past be diminished by spiritual dementia. Remember what God has done. Whatever slingshot He has placed in your hand, offer it back to Him. The only true Giant is God. David and Goliath gets retold as a motivational underdog win, but that version can miss the sharpest edge of 1 Samuel 17. David sees a blasphemer. That shift reveals the real issue is not tactics or confidence, it is whether God’s honor still matters enough to shape our courage. The passage pushes a hard question: what is worth fighting for, and what is worth risking your life to do? title: An Unlikely King Part 2 (I Samuel 16:1-13)
description: Share a comment   A king is chosen while another king still rules, and almost nobody in the room understands what just happened. We head to Bethlehem with Samuel as God stages a decision that feels backwards to human instincts: not a warrior, not the most impressive brother, not the obvious résumé. The tension is real, too. Saul’s reign is unraveling, enemies are nearby, and a public announcement would look like treason. So the whole moment comes wrapped in the ordinary cover of a sacrifice and a meal, with a quiet conversation between God and his prophet guiding every step.   We watch Samuel do what we still do today: reach for the “tallest Eliab” because he looks like leadership. Then God drops the line that flips the entire selection process on its head: people look on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart. From there we connect the text to modern appearance bias, the way image can distort hiring, promotion, and even spiritual influence. If you’ve ever felt pressured to perform a look, a vibe, or a brand, this conversation cuts through the noise.   David’s part is almost shocking in its simplicity. He’s left with the sheep, brought in late, anointed with no fanfare, and sent right back into obscurity for years. That long gap becomes the point: God manufactures a disciple over time, using rejection, repetitive work, and lonely reflection to form a leader who can bear real weight. If you feel overlooked or stuck in the mundane, Bethlehem has something to say to you. title: One Nation Under Greed (Exodus 20:17)
description: Share a comment   Your life can feel perfectly content until one moment of comparison flips the switch: their car, their house, their promotion, their marriage, their lifestyle. We take that familiar spark of jealousy and follow it to its source, because the Bible names it with uncomfortable clarity: covetousness, a greed-shaped “passion for possessing” that pulls our attention into “I, me, mine” and quietly trains us to live for more.  We walk through the Tenth Commandment in Exodus 20 and show why “You shall not covet” is not mainly about what your hands do, but what your heart rehearses in secret. From there, we move into Luke 12 where Jesus warns us to be on guard against every form of greed and tells the parable of the rich fool. The problem is not that the man has wealth; it is that he forgets his neighbor, ignores his mortality, and lives as if God is not part of the equation. The result is a life stocked with goods but starved of meaning.  Then we connect the dots people often miss: anxiety and worry can be downstream of materialism. Jesus’ words about ravens and lilies become a diagnostic test for our priorities. What matters more to us right now, getting more financially or growing spiritually? title: Cosmetics for the Tongue! (Exodus 20:16)
description: Share a comment   We’ve all done it: we walk into prayer or worship with our hands metaphorically behind our backs, clinging to something we refuse to surrender. That’s not just a private struggle, it’s a truth problem and Scripture treats it with surprising seriousness. When we “regard iniquity” and keep pretending, God isn’t impressed by the performance. He waits for repentance and real honesty.  From there we open Exodus 20:16, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” and we push it past the courtroom into everyday life. We talk about the regulation of speech in the Bible, why Leviticus links this command to slander, and how the tongue can mend a marriage or tear it apart. We also name nine common “lies of the tongue,” including lies told from fear, for profit, through silence, by exaggeration, and the most dangerous kind: lying to God while acting spiritual.  We also dig into why lies do so much damage: they expose hypocrisy (James), they fracture friendships (Proverbs), they block unity in the church (Colossians), and they invite God’s wrath. Then we turn practical with “cosmetics for the tongue” and everyday phrases that carry grace: “please,” “thank you,” “I appreciate you,” “I’m sorry,” “I forgive you,” and “I’m praying for you,” spoken with sincerity and love.  If you care about biblical truth, Christian communication, healthy relationships, and a church culture with real unity, this one is for you. title: A Thief in the Light (Exodus 20:15)
description: Share a comment   The eighth commandment sounds like it belongs in a courtroom, but Scripture aims it straight at the heart. We start with the chilling honesty of Acts 5, where Ananias and Sapphira try to look generous while hiding the truth, and the whole church feels the fallout. That scene sets the tone for a bigger question we all have to face: can we look like people of light while practicing hidden forms of stealing?   From Exodus 20:15 we track three Bible categories that expand “theft” far beyond cash. We talk about deceit as misrepresentation for unjust gain, how Romans 1 treats deception as a symptom of a God-rejecting culture, and why the church can’t afford to normalize it. Then we turn to false teaching, using 2 Corinthians 11 and Jeremiah 23 to sharpen discernment: when someone claims “God told me” while sidestepping the Word of God, they’re not offering extra insight, they’re stealing authority and attention that belong to the Lord. We also confront self-deception from James 1, where hearing without obeying becomes a quiet way to rob ourselves of integrity and growth.   The conversation gets uncomfortably practical with “defrauding” in daily relationships: wages owed for honest work, care owed to parents, intimacy owed within marriage, and even the way believers handle disputes. We close by naming theft that hides in plain sight, stealing worship from God, time from our families, and spiritual gifts from our church community, and we end with Ephesians 4’s simple reset: stop stealing, work honestly, and learn to share. title: Caging the Beast Within (Exodus 20:14)
description: Share a comment   A culture can’t stay free for long when it loses restraint, and restraint doesn’t last when revelation gets dismissed. We start with Proverbs 29:18 and follow the logic all the way into daily life: when the authority of Scripture is replaced by public opinion, soft theology, endless Christian hot takes, or the false comfort of “nothing happened, so it must be fine,” moral clarity collapses. And once moral clarity collapses, the church doesn’t just lose its message, it loses credibility.  From there we get painfully specific about sexual sin and moral purity. The command “You shall not commit adultery” isn’t treated as a narrow rule for “other people.” We talk about how temptation grows: the capability in the flesh, the private creation in the mind, the moment your senses get hooked, and the way unchecked desire starts steering your future. Proverbs makes the costs concrete, not theoretical: immorality steals from a spouse or future spouse, it dulls judgment until smart people act foolishly, and it can hollow out character from the inside.  We also leave room for hope that isn’t vague. Forgiveness is real, cleansing is complete, and change is possible when we stop renaming sin and start confessing it. We close with a workable framework for lasting victory: decide to abstain, build discipline through God’s Word and wise boundaries, and depend on the Holy Spirit day by day. title: Sunday . . . Holy Day or Holiday (Exodus 20:8-11)
description: Share a comment   If your week is ruled by deadlines, ambition, and the quiet fear of falling behind, you already know how easy it is to turn productivity into identity. We name that pressure out loud and challenge the story our culture tells: you are not significant because of what you produce or what you accomplish. We argue for a different center of gravity, a Christian identity grounded in who you are in Christ Jesus, and we explain why a weekly rhythm of rest is not weakness but wisdom.  We walk through the warning signs of workaholism, from unchanging schedules to an inability to say no, and we connect that pace to the way our bodies and souls eventually revolt. Then we open the Bible to Exodus 20 and the fourth commandment, “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy,” showing how God bakes a maintenance schedule into human life. God does not rest because he is tired; he rests to set an example for finite people who live like they are omnipotent.  We also tackle a common question with clear Scripture: why do Christians worship on Sunday instead of Saturday? We trace the Sabbath as a covenant sign for Israel (Ezekiel 20), the setting aside of that sign amid rebellion (Hosea 2), and the New Testament pattern of the Lord’s Day shaped by the resurrection, Pentecost, and early church practice (Acts 20:7). From there, we get practical: what a set-apart day looks like, why rest must include physical, emotional, and spiritual change, and how worship strengthens, cleanses, refocuses, and encourages a busy congregation. title: Posting Guards . . . Seasoning Words (Exodus 20:7)
description: Share a comment   Some words are so familiar we stop hearing them, until we realize they’ve been shaping us the whole time. title: No Props, Please! (Exodus 20, Romans 1)
description: Share a comment   If you think idolatry is only about ancient statues, this message will challenge you in the most personal way. The episode closes with a clear New Testament aim: guard your heart from idols and give Jesus Christ first place in everything. title: Ten Commandments and the 21st Century (Exodus 20:1-6)
description: Share a comment   Ever notice how easily “God” turns into a supporting character in our story? We open Exodus 20 by slowing down at the starting line, where God names Himself, asserts His authority, and reminds Israel that He redeemed them from slavery. That context changes everything: the Ten Commandments are not dusty relics or cultural leftovers. They reveal God’s holiness, confront our favorite excuses, and push us toward the only One who fulfills the law perfectly, Jesus Christ.  We unpack why God gives the law in the first place: to display His glory, to expose human sin with uncomfortable clarity, and to provide a standard for godly living. Along the way we talk about what the law cannot do, it cannot justify you, cannot produce righteousness, and cannot give real peace. If you’ve ever been intimidated by the “moral” person who seems fine without Christ, we explain why appearances can’t heal the conscience, and why the gospel is not an upgrade but a rescue.  Then we camp on the first commandment, “You shall have no other gods before me,” and show why it functions as the foundation for the other nine. We also challenge five common distortions that derail faith: God as an eager bellhop, a stern teacher, an impersonal scientist, a doting grandfather, or a Mr. Fixit we use when life breaks. If you’re wrestling with honesty, coveting, or contentment, we connect those struggles to where allegiance truly sits. title: The Sinai Summit (Exodus 19)
description: Share a comment   Smoke rolls over the mountain, lightning splits the sky, and a trumpet blast grows louder until it feels impossible to ignore. That’s the scene at Mount Sinai and it’s also the doorway into a question that hits home fast: what does it really look like to meet with God, not casually, but with reverence that changes us?  We walk through Exodus 19 to see why the Sinai summit happens in the first place. God starts with a review of grace, carrying His people like an eagle, then calls for a real response of obedience and faithfulness within the Mosaic covenant. Along the way we unpack what it means to belong to God instead of treating Him like someone who exists to serve our plans. The covenant language reveals identity and purpose: God’s treasured possession, a kingdom of priests who represent Him and intercede for others, and a holy nation set apart for His name.  From there we get very practical about “summit meetings” with God today: choosing a quiet place, coming with a prepared mind, and cultivating a teachable heart that doesn’t just hear Scripture but listens and obeys. We also name the common blockers that keep Bible study inconsistent motivation, priority, technique, and apathy and connect it to daily battles with temptation, including how Jesus answered temptation with Deuteronomy. We end by holding two truths together: God is approachable through Jesus Christ, and God is still holy enough to produce awe and trembling. title: Meekness . . . Synonym for Moses (Selected Scriptures)
description: Share a comment   Getting slapped in public is the kind of moment that reveals what is really in us. Stephen Davy opens with a story from his teen years: a stranger strikes his father, and instead of striking back, his father answers with calm control. That single response becomes a window into a biblical word most of us misunderstand, because meekness is not weakness. It is strength under control, guided by a heart submitted to the Holy Spirit.  We step away from Exodus for a focused look at the one quality Scripture uniquely highlights in only two men: Moses and Jesus Christ. Walking through key passages in Galatians 5, Colossians 3, Psalms 25, and 1 Peter 3, we trace meekness as both fruit and virtue, something God calls “precious” and something we intentionally “put on” as we mature. Then we watch it play out in real life: Moses facing family criticism in Numbers 12 without self-defense, and Jesus inviting the weary to His yoke in Matthew 11 with gentle authority that brings true spiritual rest.  The second half turns into a practical meekness test for everyday relationships: how we correct people who oppose us (2 Timothy 2), live with an unbelieving spouse (1 Peter 3), speak to skeptics with gentleness and reverence, receive hard truth from Scripture (James 1), restore someone caught in sin (Galatians 6), protect church unity (Ephesians 4), and respond to an antagonistic culture with consideration (Titus 3). If you want a Christian perspective on conflict resolution, spiritual maturity, and Christlike character, this teaching will recalibrate your tone and your instincts. title: Burnout (Exodus 18)
description: Share a comment   Running on empty can look like faithfulness until it starts breaking you and the people you’re trying to serve. We open Exodus 18 and sit in the dust outside Moses’ tent as the line grows longer, the days get heavier, and leadership becomes a one-man bottleneck. Then Jethro shows up, not just with a reunion and kind words, but with the rare mix every leader needs: encouragement, worship, and the courage to say what no one else will.  We talk about burnout in ministry and everyday leadership, why “there’s a need, so I can’t say no” quietly becomes a trap, and how doing everything yourself doesn’t actually help people. Jethro names the fallout plainly: Moses is overwhelmed, the community is neglected, and future leaders are overlooked. From there, we pull out a simple job description for spiritual leadership that still cuts through the noise: pray and teach. We dig into why teaching has to connect Scripture to real life, not just special occasions, and why prayer can’t be the task we squeeze in after the “real work.”  Finally, we unpack what to look for when you delegate: people who fear God, love truth, and live with integrity. That kind of team shares the burden, builds endurance, develops new leaders, and brings peace back to the people. If your calendar is crowded but your essentials are slipping, this is your nudge to reassess. title: Grumbling at God (Exodus 15:22-17:7)
description: Share a comment   Grumbling is rarely about water or food; it’s about what we believe when life gets tight. When the pressure rises, a single question surfaces in the heart: Is the Lord among us or not? We follow Israel’s wilderness journey right after the Red Sea and watch how quickly celebration turns into complaint, not to shame them, but to recognize ourselves with uncomfortable clarity.   We walk through three major moments from Exodus: bitter water at Marah, daily manna and quail in the wilderness, and water flowing from a struck rock. Each scene highlights God’s provision and exposes a repeated reflex to exaggerate conditions, romanticize the past, resist God’s commands, and even accuse leaders with distorted logic. Along the way, we connect the dots to 1 Corinthians 10 and why these stories are preserved as examples for New Testament believers who want a life that pleases God.   The conversation turns practical and personal: how do we overcome the slow “disease” of complaining before it masters us? We point to a steady dependence on Jesus, using John 6 where Christ calls Himself the Bread of Life, and we talk about gratitude as a learned discipline, not a personality trait. Colossians challenges us to practice being thankful, especially in the wilderness seasons where it takes real effort.   If you’ve been stuck in negativity, anxiety, or cynicism, listen through and let the central question reframe your week. title: On the Bank of the Deep Red Sea (Exodus 13-14)
description: Share a comment   You can do everything “right” and still end up in a corner with nowhere to go. That’s the tension at the Red Sea, and it’s why this teaching hits so close to home for anyone facing anxiety, conflict, financial pressure, or a decision that feels impossible.  We walk through Exodus 13 to 15, starting with the surprising calm of Israel’s departure and the detail that they carry Joseph’s bones, a reminder that God keeps promises down to the smallest piece. From there, the story tightens: Pharaoh’s elite chariots pursue, God leads his people into what looks like a dead end, and the emotional spiral kicks in fast: fear, blame, despair. We connect that pattern to the way we talk when we panic, how we seek help everywhere except the right place, and how doubt grows when we keep repeating worst-case stories out loud.  At the center is Moses’ clear fourfold exhortation for crisis moments: do not fear, stand still, watch for the Lord’s salvation, and keep quiet while the Lord fights for you. Then we track the miracle itself with fresh eyes: the protective pillar, the strong east wind, the divided sea, and the collapse of Egypt’s pursuit. The big takeaway is simple but challenging: God sometimes leads us into difficulty to develop trust, and when he comes through, the only honest response is worship and praise.  If you’re standing on the bank of your own Red Sea, press play and take these steps with us. title: Life or Death . . . At Midnight (Exodus 11-12)
description: Share a comment   Midnight is not a vibe, it’s a deadline. We step into Exodus 11 and 12 and try to feel what Israel felt: wake the kids, get dressed, eat fast with your shoes on, and be ready to move with no map. The story of the tenth plague is familiar to many, but we slow it down and ask why God calls it the final stroke, why Pharaoh’s “protection” collapses, and why this night becomes the turning point that creates a nation and resets the calendar.  From there, we dig into the Passover lamb with clear, practical language: substitution, symbolism, protection, and submission. The lamb must be without blemish, its blood must be applied, and the household must trust God’s word enough to obey detailed instructions. We talk about why the fire matters, why “when I see the blood” is the hinge of the whole event, and why the inside of the house is not the test. That one line confronts our habit of trying to bring God a stack of deeds and call it safety.  We also lean into the family side of the Passover, because God builds the story for children to ask, “What does this mean?” That becomes a challenge to explain faith with meaning, not empty ritual. We close with a gripping historical story that exposes the emptiness of self-salvation and leaves a direct question on the table: are you trusting your hands, or the Lamb? title: The Battle Between the Gods (Exodus 7-10)
description: Share a comment   Pharaoh has evidence stacked to the ceiling and still refuses to bend. That’s the tension we sit in as we keep walking through Exodus 7 to 10, where Moses and Aaron confront the most powerful ruler in the ancient world and Yahweh answers with signs that are anything but random. The plagues hit the Nile, homes, bodies, livestock, crops, and even the sun itself and we trace how each judgment exposes the emptiness of Egypt’s gods and the fragility of Pharaoh’s self-made divinity.   We talk through the phrase about God hardening Pharaoh’s heart, not as God inventing evil in a man, but as God bringing out what was already lodged there: stubborn pride that will not humble itself. From the staff becoming a crocodile to the magicians admitting “This is the finger of God,” the pattern is clear: counterfeit power can imitate for a moment, but it cannot stand. Along the way, we highlight the turning point where Goshen is protected, making the spiritual line unmistakable between God’s people and Egypt’s oppression.   Then we bring it home with two personal lessons that land hard: obeying God may not bring the relief you expect, and serving God may not bring immediate results. If we build our faith on comfort or visible wins, we will quit when the pressure rises. If we build it on God’s glory, we can stay steady even when the frogs are still croaking. title: God's Best . . . When Things Couldn't Be Worse! (Exodus 4:27-7:7)
description: Share a comment   Obedience is supposed to make things better, right? Moses walks into Pharaoh’s court with a clear word from God and walks out to find Israel’s workload doubled, their hope evaporating, and their leaders spitting blame in his face. We sit with that brutal turn in Exodus 5 and the very human crash that follows when your best efforts seem to trigger the opposite result.   From Pharaoh’s ego to the no straw brick quota, the pressure is designed to break a people and silence worship. We talk through why disappointment often shows up right after a moment of real spiritual momentum, and why Moses’ next move matters so much: he returns to the Lord with his questions instead of walking away hardened. That single choice becomes the hinge between bitterness and maturity.   God’s response is not a step-by-step tactic but a revelation of identity and power. The repeated “I am the Lord” and the cascade of “I will” promises reshape the whole story, moving the weight off Moses’ ability and onto God’s character, sovereignty, and faithfulness. We also draw out a simple application that hits close to home: affliction produces wisdom, and wisdom learns to trust the invisible hand of a God who keeps his word. title: Availability . . . and a Game of Chess (Exodus 3-4:17)
description: Share a comment   God calls Moses out of an ordinary day and into a moment that changes everything: a burning bush, holy ground, and a mission Moses does not want. What follows isn’t just ancient history, it’s a painfully familiar pattern of hesitation. We hear Moses reach for excuse after excuse, and we recognize ourselves in the questions: Who am I to do this? What if I don’t have the answers? What if people don’t believe me? What if I’m not gifted enough to speak or lead?  We trace each objection and God’s response, because the story is packed with practical guidance for Christian leadership, calling, and everyday faith. God doesn’t build Moses with flattering words or promise a perfectly easy path. He offers presence: “I will be with you.” He reveals His name, Yahweh, “I AM,” and shows that spiritual authority comes less from having a polished method and more from knowing God deeply. We also connect that revelation to Jesus’ words in John 8, pointing to the heart of discipleship: learning Christ, not just collecting answers.  Then the tension rises as Moses claims inability and inadequacy, and God answers with undeniable signs and a blunt reminder that He made Moses’ mouth. The conversation lands on the moment where excuses turn into refusal, and we bring it home through Matthew 28 and the Great Commission: Christ gives the authority, the message, and the promise of His presence. If you’ve been stalling, bargaining, or waiting for “someone else” to step up, this is your nudge to stop playing chess with God and surrender. title: Desert Lab 101 (Exodus 2:15-22)
description: Share a comment   Failure has a way of making life feel like a desert, silent, exposed, and endless. We lean into three of Scripture’s most relatable “blown it” moments and ask a different question than “How did they mess up?” We ask: What did God build in them afterward, and what can He build in us when we’re tempted to quit, hide, or numb the guilt?  We walk through John Mark’s story in Acts, the young helper with every advantage who deserts the mission and becomes a point of sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas. From there we widen the lens to the pressure points most of us actually face: fear of ridicule, the ease of keeping quiet about Jesus, and the moment where convenience starts to look like wisdom. It’s a practical conversation about Christian perseverance, courage, and why spiritual potential means little without endurance.  Then we turn to David, not as a coward but as a man crushed by moral failure, and we sit with the raw honesty of Psalm 32 and the turning point of Psalm 51. Finally, we revisit Moses, trained for leadership yet forced into Midian’s obscurity, where self-sufficiency dies and dependence on God is born. A surprising thread ties it all together: God often speaks in the desert through another believer, a Peter, a Jethro, a timely voice you’re meant to hear.  If you’re walking through regret, disappointment, or spiritual dryness, this is a reminder that the desert doesn’t have to be the end of your story. title: Forty Years Ahead of God (Exodus 2:11-15; Acts 7:21-29)
description: Share a comment   A single sentence can expose an entire life plan. When Moses steps into a fight and tries to position himself as Israel’s deliverer, the response is sharp: “Who made you a ruler and judge over us?” We follow that question through Acts 7 and Exodus 2 to uncover what goes wrong when calling turns into self-appointment, and when passion tries to replace God’s authority.  We talk through Moses’ unique preparation in Egypt, his education, influence, and leadership potential, then the moment he “looks this way and that” and chooses a method God never asked for. The result is a sobering case study in getting ahead of God: serving God while ignoring God, using pragmatic tactics that seem to work, and discovering you can be right about the need and wrong about the timing. Along the way, we connect Moses’ shortcut to the New Testament pattern of spiritual warfare in 1 Timothy 2, where Paul calls believers to prayer even under corrupt and violent leadership.  We also bring it home with three concrete questions for Christian decision making and spiritual leadership: Is impatience shaping your choices, are you violating God’s counsel to get what you want, and are you planning everywhere but up? If you’re facing a big decision, building a ministry, or feeling the pressure to act now, this conversation will slow you down in the best way. title: Faith . . . and a Wicker Basket (Exodus 2:1-10)
description: Share a comment   A government order turns newborn life into a death sentence, and suddenly Exodus 2 feels less like a children’s story and more like a survival account. We walk through Moses’ rescue with fresh eyes, noticing a detail most people skip: the major characters stay unnamed for a long stretch, as if Scripture is quietly insisting that God is the lead actor, not the supporting cast.   We trace the faith of Amram and Jochebed as something sturdier than optimism: they hide a baby for three months, then build a waterproof basket, choose the placement, and send Miriam to watch with a line ready at the right moment. We also explore the strange providence of Pharaoh’s daughter bathing in the Nile as a religious fertility ritual, and how a crying child and a compassionate heart collide at the only point in the kingdom where Pharaoh’s edict can be overridden. Along the way we connect the story to Acts 7 and Hebrews 11 to frame the whole scene as faith in action.   Then we bring it home with three takeaways that cut close: faith benefits the people nearest to us, faith should shape everyday decisions and integrity, and faith impacts the observers we never knew were watching. The episode even follows the thread of Pharaoh’s daughter beyond the riverbank, raising the question of how living faith can ripple outward for decades. title: From Pasture to Brickyard (Exodus 1:1-22)
description: Share a comment   A nation grows, a ruler panics, and cruelty becomes “policy.” We open Exodus 1 with the uncomfortable logic of fear: a new Pharaoh forgets Joseph, looks at Israel’s strength, and decides the only safe future is control. That decision spirals fast, from hard labor and forced building projects to covert orders aimed at newborns. The ancient details are vivid, but the questions feel modern: what happens when power is driven by insecurity, and what does it do to a society’s moral compass?  We trace the three escalating plans Pharaoh uses against the Hebrews, then slow down at the turning point in the story: two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, who “fear God” and refuse to participate in evil. Their courage becomes a practical framework for conscience, authority, and civil disobedience. We talk about the cost of saying no, why integrity is more than a private virtue, and how faith shows up when the pressure is real, whether that pressure comes from leaders, institutions, or the crowd.  The conversation also draws a straight line from Exodus to the bigger biblical story of redemption, pointing to Moses as deliverer and the way Exodus foreshadows rescue from sin through Jesus Christ. We end with two grounded takeaways for anyone walking through suffering: affliction can be unfair yet purposeful, and when God seems absent He is always at work. If you need a final image to hold onto, it’s the story of a child carrying a heavy basket with confidence because his father knows his limits. title: Hand in Glove (Romans 8:12–15)
description: Share a comment   A glove can point, clap, and wave all day long but only when a hand fills it. That’s the picture we keep coming back to as we walk through Romans 8: the Christian life is not powered by grit, personality, or religious hustle. We’re “willing gloves,” and the Holy Spirit is the One who indwells, energizes, and directs us so our lives actually move in a new direction.  We get practical about a question that confuses a lot of people: what does it mean to be led by the Spirit? We challenge the popular idea that spiritual guidance is mainly a mystical feeling, a private voice, or the latest trend of dream-based direction. When “God told me” becomes more exciting than what God has already said, the result is distraction and instability. We read the warning signs, talk about how false confidence can grow, and why Scripture sufficiency matters for everyday discernment.  Then we lay out a clearer definition: being led by the Spirit means being led into the Word of God and into obedience to the Word of God. From there, Romans 8 opens up the relief of adoption as sons and daughters, not slavery and fear, but full family rights and a real inheritance. That new relationship changes our prayer life too, giving us the freedom to cry, “Abba, Father,” with intimacy and reverence.  If you want biblical guidance, deeper assurance, and a steadier approach to Spirit-led living, press play.
